text: I'm just wondering how or if my marriage can move forward after my wife's affair of over six years. One of my really, really good buddies that I grew up with, I just found out recently, was also involved. This was two weeks ago. I found that out. So she and him messed around recently. Good God, dude. I mean, your wife slept with your friends back and forth a lot of them for a long, long time. So it's not like she fell in love with somebody, made a terrible long-term mistake. She is a liar. That's who she is in her soul. I gave it a couple of weeks to cool off and just said like, hey, I just need full transparency, just so that I know, because I don't want to be walking around talking to these guys, continuing to hang out with these guys when there's been more, right? She's lost any benefit of the doubt. That's gone. If you want to save it, here's what has to happen. You have to completely 100% clear the deck. Your old marriage is gone, does not exist, period. And then you have to give her a super clear path back to reestablishing trust. Back to reestablishing trust after his wife has been cheating on him for six years with multiple partners, including close friends? Back to reestablishing trust? You see, guys, this is my problem with modern psychologists, therapists, and shrinks in general. The vast majority of them, in my humble opinion, quite often give advice that makes people's lives worse rather than better. This is John Deloney, probably one of the most famous mental and emotional health experts out there. Millions of subscribers, bestselling author, host of his own show. And this is the advice that he gives to this guy. And to be fair here, I actually don't think that John Deloney is that bad overall. I've watched quite a few of his videos and found myself agreeing with him on certain things. But even if a relatively good counselor like him gives such bad advice in a situation like this, just imagine the level of incompetence of others who are much worse. So let me be clear. I don't think that the mental and emotional health industry is bad overall. Of course not. But like in many other industries, you need to be very, very careful about which specialists you go to. And you need to use your own common sense when you receive advice from them. In this case, it is hard to find a simpler situation. The wife has been cheating for years with multiple people, including close friends. There is no reestablishing trust. There is no coming back. He needs to end it with her completely. No contact at all. And all these guys around him are not his friends either. He needs to cut them off as well. If it would make things easier for him, he might even need to move to another city and start his life from scratch. New job, new social circle, maybe new hobbies. And most importantly, he needs to start working on his boundaries, on self-respect, on self-worth, self-love. Because that is where the real problem lies. Until he starts respecting himself, how can he expect other people to respect him? This is the kind of advice he actually needs if he wants even a chance at having a decent life. Not the hell he is in right now. And I partly understand why some therapists give advice like you need to reestablish trust. Because it is a much simpler advice than you need to rebuild your life from ground up. But the only way to get to a better life is through a lot of very, very hard work. There is no magic pill here.
